name: Stone tools
note: Who made the oldest tools is not known: Australopithecus afarensis, Kenyanthropus platyops or a species not yet identified.

name: Control of fire
note: Claims reach back 1.5 to 2 million years, but traces of wood ash from about 1 million years ago are the evidence with the firmest scholarly support.

name: Pottery
independent_origins: Ounjougou, Mali by 9400 BCE; Brazil 9,500–5,000 years ago
note: Fired-clay figurines are older: those of Dolní Věstonice in the Czech Republic date to 29,000–25,000 BCE.

name: Potter's wheel
note: Many scholars credit the Sumerians of Mesopotamia; south-eastern Europe, China and Egypt have also been proposed.

name: Copper smelting
independent_origins: the Andes; the Aïr Mountains, Niger 3000–2500 BCE
note: A copper axe from Prokuplje in Serbia may be older, c. 5500 BCE, and smelting may have begun separately in Asia and in Europe.

name: Iron smelting
note: Other early claims are tentative or disputed, at Kaman-Kalehöyük in Turkey (2200–2000 BCE) and Lejja in Nigeria; the old idea of a Hittite monopoly on iron-working is no longer accepted.

name: Glassmaking
note: The earliest glass objects are often counted as faience; true glass appears in the 15th century BCE.

name: Cast iron
note: Whether Europe's blast furnaces of the 12th and 13th centuries arose independently or from Chinese knowledge is uncertain.

name: Crucible steel
note: Securely proven production sites are later: Sri Lanka in the 6th to 10th centuries CE and southern India from the 16th; the early evidence from Kodumanal is preliminary.

name: Bessemer process
note: The American William Kelly is said to have found the process in 1851; whether both men invented the same process is disputed.

name: Porcelain
note: By stricter definitions, whiteness and translucency, porcelain begins in the late Sui and early Tang; Shang dynasty wares are called proto-porcelain.

name: Papermaking
note: Paper is traditionally credited to the court official Cai Lun in 105 CE, but older paper has been found, so its first date and inventor are unknown.

name: Silk
note: A Confucian text dates silk to about 2700 BCE; archaeology points to the Yangshao period, 5000–3000 BCE.

name: Spinning wheel
note: Its origin is disputed: Kuhn and Cheng argue for China, where dictionaries of the 2nd century CE mention it; others place it in India, or in the Middle East, where it was known by 1030.

name: Spinning jenny
note: Thomas Highs of Leigh has claimed to be the inventor, and a myth credits Thomas Earnshaw with a similar device that he destroyed.

name: Jacquard machine
note: The article says the machine was based on earlier inventions by Basile Bouchon (1725), Jean Baptiste Falcon (1728) and Jacques Vaucanson (1740), that Jacquard 'possibly combined mechanical elements of other inventors, but certainly innovated', and that a first prototype of a Jacquard-type loom was made in the second half of the 15th century by an Italian weaver known as Jean le Calabrais.

name: Cotton gin
note: The modern cotton gin is credited to Eli Whitney in 1793, though some credit Catharine Littlefield Greene with suggesting its brush.

name: Eyeglasses
note: A 17th-century claim that Salvino degli Armati of Florence invented them is false, and the suggested Chinese and Indian origins rest on later evidence.

name: Mechanical clock
note: Derek de Solla Price held that the water-driven escapements of Tang China, built in 723–725, were the source of the Western escapement.

name: Agriculture
independent_origins: the Yangtze, China 13,500–8,200 years ago; northern China c. 6000 BCE; New Guinea perhaps 8000 BCE; Mesoamerica c. 7000 BCE; eastern North America c. 2500 BCE; Ethiopia, the Sahel and West Africa
note: Dates for its beginning in West Asia range from about 12,000 to 8000 BCE.

name: Domestication of animals
independent_origins: the Fertile Crescent (goats, pigs, sheep, cattle) 11,000–10,000 years ago; East Asia (pigs) 8,000 years ago

name: Rice
independent_origins: West Africa (African rice) about 3,000 years ago
note: Estimates for its domestication in China range from 13,500 to 8,200 years ago.

name: Potato
place: Lake Titicaca region, Peru and Bolivia

name: Plough
note: Ox-drawn ards may go back to the 6th millennium BCE in Mesopotamia and the Indus Valley.

name: Qanat
note: Some sources propose an origin in south-east Arabia, and the dating of the Peruvian puquios is disputed.

name: Chinampa
note: Culhuacan may have built the first chinampas about 1100; the Aztecs did not invent them but farmed them on a far larger scale.

name: Andean terraces
note: The origin of terracing in the Andes is poorly understood.

name: Seed drill
note: The first single-tube seed drills may go back to Sumer.

name: Horse collar
note: An earlier, doubtful depiction comes from a 3rd-century tomb in Sichuan, and some see a partial collar in ancient Rome.

name: Beer
note: How beer was first made is debated; the earliest chemically confirmed barley beer, from Godin Tepe in Iran, is 5,400–5,000 years old.

name: Tea
note: Tea drinking may be far older, under the Shang and in Yunnan, but early words for it are uncertain, and its discovery by Shennong is legend.

name: Refrigeration
note: Jacob Perkins built the first working vapour-compression system in 1834, and James Harrison the first practical one in 1851.

name: Green Revolution
note: The article's lead says the changes first emerged in developed countries in the early 20th century, while its history dates the genesis to Henry A. Wallace's visit to Mexico in 1940; the term itself was first used by William S. Gaud on 8 March 1968.

name: Arch
note: H. V. Hilprecht dated the Nippur arch to before 4000 BCE.

name: The first stone pyramid
note: Some Egyptologists think the nearby enclosure wall Gisr el-Mudir is older; the credit to Imhotep is that of modern Egyptologists.

name: Aqueduct
note: Early aqueducts were also built in the Indian subcontinent, Greece, the Near East and the Nile valley.

name: Roman concrete
place: Rome (first in the harbours near Baiae)
note: Some scholars think it was developed a century earlier.

name: Dome
note: When the first dome was built is not known; the mammoth-bone dwellings of Mezhirich may be the earliest. Corbelled stone domes appear in the Neolithic Near East.

name: Suspension bridge
note: No date for the first bridges is known; they were part of the road system of the Inca Empire (1438–1533).

name: Pound lock
note: Diodorus Siculus credits engineers of Ptolemy II with a lock in Egypt about 274 BCE, but not a pound lock.

name: Grand Canal
note: Its oldest sections were dug by the states of Wu and Yue from 486 BCE; Emperor Yang of Sui joined them into one network in 604–609.

name: Segmental arch bridge
note: No record from the time of its building survives; the credit to Li Chun comes from later chronicles.

name: Lighthouse
note: Pliny the Elder named Sostratus of Cnidus as its architect, but that is disputed.

name: Stepwell
note: The earliest traces are at Dholavira, a city of the Indus Valley Civilisation; Ashoka’s inscriptions describe stepwells along the roads, and the first rock-cut ones date from 200–400 CE.

name: Safety elevator
note: A safety device already featured in Gaetano Genovese’s “flying chair” at Caserta in 1845.

name: Skyscraper
note: Which building came first is debated: some point to Philadelphia’s Jayne Building (1849–50) or New York’s Equitable Life Building (1870).

name: Water wheel
note: The first watermills have been placed in Persia before 350 BCE and in Byzantium and Alexandria in the 3rd century BCE.

name: Windmill
note: Whether the vertical windmill of 12th-century Europe owed anything to the Persian one is unclear.

name: Coal
note: Neanderthals may have burned lignite at Les Canalettes in France about 70,000 years ago.

name: Aeolipile
note: Vitruvius described aeolipiles earlier, about 30–20 BCE; both drew on the work of Ctesibius.

name: Steam engine
credited_to: Habsburg Spain; Kingdom of Great Britain
people: Jerónimo de Ayanz y Beaumont; Thomas Savery; Thomas Newcomen
note: Ayanz patented a steam-powered pump in 1606; Thomas Savery’s pump of 1698 was the first commercial steam device, and Thomas Newcomen’s engine of about 1712 the first to drive machinery.

name: Electric generator
note: The self-excited dynamo was invented independently by Wheatstone, Siemens and Varley in 1866–1867.

name: Internal combustion engine
note: John Barber’s gas turbine of 1791 came earlier; Nicolaus Otto’s four-stroke engine of 1876 was the first modern one.

name: Electric light
people: Humphry Davy; Joseph Swan; Thomas Edison
note: Credit for the first practical bulb is disputed between Thomas Edison, whose first successful test was in 1879, and Joseph Swan, whose bulbs were in use in London by 1881.

name: Steam turbine
note: Taqi al-Din’s turbine turned a roasting spit; the modern steam turbine was invented by Charles Parsons in 1884.

name: Oil well
note: The first modern oil wells were drilled near Baku in 1846–1848.

name: Solar cell
note: The first practical solar cell was demonstrated at Bell Laboratories in 1954.

name: Wheel
note: Wheeled vehicles appear almost together in Mesopotamia, the Caucasus and Europe in the 4th millennium BCE; whether they spread from the Near East is debated.

name: Sail
independent_origins: Taiwan and Island Southeast Asia (Austronesian sails) c. 3000 BCE
note: When and where the sail was invented is not known; many date it no earlier than the 5th millennium BCE.

name: Domestication of the horse
note: Earlier claims, at Botai in Kazakhstan (3700–3500 BCE) and on the steppe in the 5th millennium BCE, are debated.

name: Chariot
note: Some scholars class the Sintashta vehicles as carts and see the chariot as a Near Eastern invention of the early 2nd millennium BCE.

name: Outrigger canoe
note: Outriggers may first have been needed after the crab claw sail appeared, around 1500 BCE.

name: Stirrup
note: Toe loops were used in India by the 2nd century BCE, some credit the Sarmatians, and a single iron stirrup from Mongolia is dated 243–405 CE.

name: Lateen sail
note: An older view gave it an eastern origin, in Arab seafaring.

name: Sternpost rudder
note: Some count the steering oars of Egypt and Rome as rudders; Joseph Needham held that the sternpost rudder reached Europe from China.

name: Astrolabe
note: Whether Ptolemy or earlier astronomers used it is debated, and its attribution to Hypatia rests on a misreading.

name: Magnetic compass
note: A lodestone “south-pointing spoon” for divination is attributed to the Han in the 2nd century BCE, but none has been found.

name: Caravel
credited_to: Kingdom of Portugal; Crown of Castile
note: The name covered different hulls over the centuries; the ocean-going caravel of the voyages of exploration was developed in 15th-century Portugal.

name: Marine chronometer
note: Christiaan Huygens built a balance-spring chronometer in 1675 that kept poor time at sea, and some see Pierre Le Roy’s of 1766 as the basis of the modern chronometer.

name: Steam locomotive
note: Trevithick’s Coalbrookdale locomotive of 1802 may have run earlier, but no record of it working survives.

name: Steamship
note: This was the Pyroscaphe, the first working steamboat; the first sea-going steamship, Richard Wright’s Experiment, sailed in 1813.

name: Bicycle
note: Drais’s running machine had no pedals; they were added in France in the early 1860s.

name: Automobile
note: Steam road vehicles came earlier, beginning with Nicolas-Joseph Cugnot’s of about 1769.

name: Aeroplane
note: Clément Ader’s Éole made an uncontrolled hop in 1890, and Alberto Santos-Dumont’s flight of 1906 was claimed as the first without a catapult.

name: Jet engine
note: Maxime Guillaume patented a jet engine in 1921 that was never built, and Frank Whittle patented the turbojet in England in 1930.

name: Bow and arrow
note: The earliest evidence is indirect, small stone points from Uzbekistan, Sibudu in South Africa (72,000–60,000 years ago) and elsewhere; the oldest surviving bows, from Holmegaard in Denmark, date from about 9000 BCE.

name: Composite bow
note: When and where it began is not known; the bows in the tomb of Tutankhamun, who died in 1324 BCE, are among the earliest dated.

name: Mail armour
note: Etruscan mail of the 4th century BCE is older, and the Avesta already mentions mail.

name: Trireme
note: Whether it came from Greece (Corinth, by Thucydides) or Phoenicia (Sidon) is disputed; triremes are first definitely recorded in battle about 525 BCE.

name: Catapult
note: The Bible credits King Uzziah of Judah with stone-throwing machines about 750 BCE, but in a much later text.

name: Crossbow
note: Some trace the crossbow and its name into China from Austroasiatic peoples in the 4th century BCE, but older locks from Zhou tombs contradict this.

name: Counterweight trebuchet
note: Where it was first built is not agreed: al-Tarsusi’s description of 1187 implies it was not new, and earlier cases have been argued from sieges between 1090 and 1165.

name: Greek fire
note: Fire-carrying ships may predate Kallinikos’s arrival, and some think it was the work of the chemists of Constantinople rather than one man.

name: Cannon
note: Estimates for the first true cannon run from about 1200 to 1280; the Xanadu Gun of 1298 is the oldest with a date inscribed.

name: Arquebus
note: The matchlock arquebus appeared shortly before 1475 in Europe, or by 1465 in the Ottoman Empire; its origin is disputed.

name: Musket
note: It may have been little more than a new name for a heavy arquebus; the word is recorded from 1499.

name: Turtle ship
note: Admiral Yi Sun-sin used an improved design against the Japanese invasions of 1592–1598; whether it was armoured with iron plates is disputed.

name: Ironclad warship
note: France’s armoured floating batteries of 1855 also have a claim to be the first ironclads.

name: Submarine
note: Drebbel’s oar-driven boat was a submersible; David Bushnell’s Turtle of 1775 was the first verified submarine able to move underwater on its own.

name: Tank
note: No single inventor can be named, and earlier designs, from Leonardo da Vinci’s to Lancelot de Mole’s of 1911, were never built.

name: Atomic bomb
note: It was a joint project of the United States with the United Kingdom and Canada.

name: Ishango bone
note: Its age, with estimates from 9000 BCE to 44,000 years ago, and whether its marks are mathematical are both debated.

name: Cuneiform
note: The article notes a contrarian view that the clay tokens were not the precursor of writing, and says the meaning and usage of the tokens are still a matter of debate.

name: Egyptian hieroglyphs
note: Whether hieroglyphs arose independently or from Mesopotamian writing is debated; signs from Abydos as early as 3400 BCE question Mesopotamian priority.

name: Base-60 numbers
note: Otto Neugebauer held that the origins of sexagesimal are not as simple, consistent, or singular in time as they are often portrayed, its use always mixing in a strong undercurrent of decimal notation.

name: Papyrus
note: It was used at least as far back as the First Dynasty; the oldest written papyri yet found, the Diary of Merer, date from about 2560 BCE.

name: Abacus
note: The form of the Sumerian device is unknown; the oldest surviving counting board, the Salamis Tablet, dates from about 300 BCE.

name: The first alphabet
note: An early date of about 1850 BCE and a late one of about 1550 BCE are debated, which decides whether the alphabet arose in Egypt or in Canaan.

name: Chinese writing
note: Its mature form implies earlier development, but no older writing has been found.

name: Phoenician alphabet
note: No Phoenician inscription is securely dated before the 10th century BCE.

name: Greek alphabet
note: The oldest substantial inscriptions date from about 740 BCE.

name: Brahmi script
note: Most scholars derive it from a Semitic script, usually Aramaic; earlier inscribed potsherds from Sri Lanka and Tamil Nadu are disputed.

name: Maya script
note: It was long thought that the Maya took writing from the Olmec or Epi-Olmec; murals found in 2005 make an independent invention possible.

name: Codex
note: A papyrus codex from Ptolemaic Egypt may be older.

name: Euclid's Elements
note: It is largely a compilation of earlier Greek mathematics, and how much of it Euclid wrote himself is debated.

name: Zero
independent_origins: Mesoamerica: south-central Mexico and Central America (earliest at Chiapa de Corzo, Chiapas) 36 BCE
note: Placeholder zeros are older, in Babylonian texts from about 700 BCE, and Ptolemy used a zero by 150 CE; Brahmagupta set out rules for calculating with zero in the 7th century.

name: Hindu–Arabic numerals
note: The dating of its oldest witness, the Bakhshali manuscript, is disputed; the first dated, undisputed zero is the Gwalior inscription of 876.

name: Algebra
note: Whether earlier work, from the Rhind papyrus to Diophantus and Brahmagupta, counts as algebra is debated.

name: Quipu
note: A possible proto-quipu from Caral, of 3000–1800 BCE, has yet to be evaluated.

name: Woodblock printing
note: These were prints on silk; the earliest prints on paper date from about 650–670, and the Diamond Sutra of 868 is the oldest dated printed book.

name: Movable type
note: Whether Asian movable type influenced Gutenberg is debated.

name: Hangul
note: When work on it began is unknown, and whether scripts such as ʼPhags-pa influenced its letters is debated.

name: Calculus
note: Newton derived his results in 1665–1666 but Leibniz published first, in 1684; they reached them independently, though the credit was bitterly disputed.

name: Long Count calendar
note: The earliest date is uncertain: Takalik Abaj Stela 2 may be older, and the San Bartolo text of about 300 BCE may be the earliest Long Count notation.

name: Babylonian astronomy
note: The article also gives earlier or vaguer dates, none presented as secure: lunar omens in 'reports from Nineveh and Babylon, circa 2500-670 B.C.', Venus observations that 'probably' go back to the second millennium BC but survive in a 7th-century BC copy (the Venus tablet of Ammisaduqa), and the Omen Compendia, composed from the beginning of the second millennium onwards.

name: Heliocentrism
note: Copernicus revived it as predictive astronomy in 1543; whether Aryabhata’s system of 499 was heliocentric is debated.

name: Antikythera mechanism
note: Its date and place of making are disputed: estimates run from 205 to 87 BCE, and Corinth’s colonies, Pergamon and Rhodes have been proposed.

name: Camera obscura
note: The article mentions possible earlier traces: perforated gnomons projecting a pinhole image of the sun in the Chinese Zhoubi Suanjing (1046 BC–256 BC, with material added until c. 220 AD), and theories that camera obscura effects inspired Paleolithic cave paintings or played a role in Neolithic structures.

name: Telescope
note: The actual inventor is unknown; Lipperhey’s patent application of 1608 is the earliest record of a telescope.

name: Microscope
note: The inventor is unknown; claims have been made for Zacharias Janssen in the Netherlands, for Cornelis Drebbel and for Galileo.

name: Laws of motion and gravitation
note: Robert Hooke claimed priority for the inverse-square law of gravity, which Newton denied.

name: Ulugh Beg Observatory
note: It was built to the plans of the earlier Maragheh observatory.

name: Evolution by natural selection
credited_to: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland
note: Patrick Matthew in 1831 and William Charles Wells in 1813 had anticipated natural selection.

name: Periodic table
note: Lothar Meyer’s book of 1864 and John Newlands’s work of 1863–1864 held earlier versions; Mendeleev’s was the first to be generally accepted.

name: Germ theory of disease
note: Girolamo Fracastoro proposed a basic form in 1546; the theory prevailed only after the work of Louis Pasteur and Robert Koch in the late 19th century.

name: Laws of inheritance
note: His work was rediscovered in 1900 by Hugo de Vries, Carl Correns and Erich von Tschermak.

name: Radioactivity
people: Henri Becquerel; Marie Curie; Pierre Curie

name: Theory of relativity
note: Special relativity was published in 1905, general relativity, a theory of gravitation, in 1915.

name: Quantum theory
people: Max Planck; Werner Heisenberg; Erwin Schrödinger
note: Planck’s quantum hypothesis of 1900 began it; modern quantum mechanics was formulated in 1925–1926.

name: Atomic theory
note: The idea of indivisible particles is ancient, but as philosophy rather than science.

name: Structure of DNA
people: James Watson; Francis Crick; Rosalind Franklin; Maurice Wilkins

name: Nuclear fission
people: Otto Hahn; Fritz Strassmann; Lise Meitner; Otto Robert Frisch
note: Hahn and Strassmann found the evidence in Berlin; Meitner and Frisch, who explained it in January 1939, were then in exile.

name: Cell theory
note: Schleiden claimed as his own an idea Barthélemy Dumortier had stated earlier, and Rudolf Virchow’s third tenet of 1855 had already been proposed by Robert Remak.

name: Soap
note: Who first made true soap, as distinct from earlier soap-like mixtures, is uncertain; Pliny the Elder called it an invention of the Gauls.

name: Tyrian purple
note: The Minoans may have pioneered the dye; the Phoenicians of Tyre, after whom it is named, may have used it from about 1570 BCE.

name: Alchemy
note: Whether the Western, Chinese and Indian traditions share an origin is an open question.

name: Modern chemistry
note: Recent work sees a gradual change over two centuries, with Robert Boyle laying its foundations.

name: Synthetic dye
credited_to: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland
note: Perkin found mauveine by accident while trying to make quinine.

name: Organic chemistry
note: Whether it overthrew vitalism, the source of its fame, is disputed.

name: Oil refining
note: The modern industry began with lamp oil from coal: Abraham Gesner claimed priority from 1846 and James Young patented his process in 1850.

name: Trepanation
note: Estimates of the earliest trepanation vary from 10,000 to 7,000 years ago.

name: Edwin Smith Papyrus
note: The surviving copy may reproduce an older original of the Old Kingdom; the suggestion that Imhotep wrote it is conjecture.

name: Sushruta Samhita
note: Its date is much debated: its composition may have begun in the last centuries BCE, and proposals range from 2000 BCE to the 6th century CE.

name: Hippocratic medicine
note: None of its some 60 texts is proven to be by Hippocrates himself.

name: Acupuncture
note: Its origin is disputed: some date it to about 600 BCE, and its absence from the Mawangdui texts of 198 BCE suggests a later start.

name: Hospital (bimaristan)
note: Al-Walid I’s foundation at Damascus in 707 may have been a leprosarium rather than a hospital, and Harun al-Rashid’s traditional hospital of 787 is questioned.

name: Quarantine
note: Isolating the sick is far older, from the book of Leviticus to Ibn Sina’s Canon of Medicine; Ragusa held back newcomers who might carry plague.

name: Modern anatomy
note: The more than 250 illustrations are generally attributed by modern scholars to the 'studio of Titian' rather than to Johannes Stephanus of Calcar, who drew for Vesalius's earlier tracts.

name: Circulation of the blood
note: Ibn al-Nafis had described the pulmonary circulation in the 13th century and Michael Servetus in 1553; the complete circulation is Harvey’s.

name: Quinine
note: The alkaloid itself was isolated in 1820 by Pierre Joseph Pelletier and Joseph Bienaimé Caventou; the story that the Countess of Chinchón brought the bark to Europe is a myth.

name: Variolation
note: Some sources date it to the 11th century in China, and claims of an ancient Indian origin are disputed.

name: Vaccination
note: Benjamin Jesty and others had tried cowpox inoculation from 1774; Jenner was the first to publish the evidence.

name: Anaesthesia
note: Who deserves the most credit for general anaesthesia is debated.

name: Antiseptic surgery
note: Ignaz Semmelweis showed in 1847–1848 that hand washing prevented infection; Joseph Lister popularised antiseptic surgery from 1867.

name: Pasteurisation
note: Heating wine to preserve it was known in China from 1117.

name: Aspirin
note: Bayer made it in a pure, stable form in 1897, credited to Felix Hoffmann or perhaps Arthur Eichengrün; willow bark, its natural source, has been used for at least 2,400 years.

name: Insulin
people: Frederick Banting; Charles Best; John Macleod; James Collip
note: Nicolae Paulescu in Bucharest made a pancreatic extract that lowered blood sugar in 1916, but it could not be used on people.

name: Penicillin
people: Alexander Fleming; Howard Florey; Ernst Chain
note: Reports of the antibacterial properties of Penicillium mould go back to the late 19th century, but the article says scientists could not discern what caused the effect and that Fleming was the first to show that Penicillium rubens had antibacterial properties.

name: Polio vaccine
people: Hilary Koprowski; Jonas Salk; Albert Sabin
note: Jonas Salk’s injected vaccine was shown effective in 1955; earlier vaccines of 1934–1935 were withdrawn.

name: Oral rehydration therapy
note: It came into wide use after the 1960s discovery that glucose speeds the absorption of sodium and water in cholera.

name: Coinage
note: Guanzhuang in China is the oldest securely dated minting site, and Aegina has also been proposed for the first coins.

name: Royal Road and relay posts
note: Its western sections may first have been built by the Assyrian kings.

name: Cursus publicus
note: The article allows that a courier service may have existed for a time under the Roman Republic, but says the clearest reference, by Suetonius, states that Augustus created the system.

name: Paper money
note: Merchants in Sichuan issued the first notes, the jiaozi; the government took over their production in 1023.

name: Newspaper
note: Court gazettes circulated earlier in Tang China, and a printed daily, the Jobo, appeared in Joseon Korea in 1577.

name: Optical telegraph
note: Robert Hooke outlined a visual telegraph in 1684, and the Chappe brothers first demonstrated theirs in 1791.

name: Electrical telegraph
credited_to: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland
note: Georges-Louis Le Sage had an electric telegraph working between two rooms in 1774; the first commercial system, Cooke and Wheatstone’s, dates from 1837.

name: Photography
note: The article notes that Johann Heinrich Schulze's fleeting images of stencilled letters, about 1717, are 'sometimes regarded as the very first form of photography', that Thomas Wedgwood made the first reliably documented attempt to capture camera images around 1800 but could not fix them, and that Hippolyte Bayard developed a method of his own but was not recognised as its inventor because he delayed announcing it.

name: Telephone
people: Johann Philipp Reis; Alexander Graham Bell
note: Credit is disputed among Reis, Antonio Meucci, Charles Bourseul, Elisha Gray and Alexander Graham Bell, who received the first United States patent in 1876.

name: Radio
note: Heinrich Hertz had sent radio waves through the air in 1886–1888, and Alexander Popov and Jagadish Chandra Bose demonstrated receivers in 1895.

name: Cinematograph
note: The Lumière brothers’ machine of 1895 gave the famous early screenings in Paris; the first commercial screening of films took place in New York in May 1895.

name: Television
people: Georges Rignoux; A. Fournier; John Logie Baird
note: John Logie Baird’s demonstration of 1926 is widely regarded as the first true public television demonstration.

name: ENIAC
independent_origins: Britain (Colossus) during the Second World War
note: A US court ruled in 1973 that its inventors had drawn on John Atanasoff’s Atanasoff–Berry Computer, prototyped in 1939.

name: Transistor
people: John Bardeen; Walter Brattain; William Shockley
note: The concept of a field-effect transistor had been patented earlier by Julius Edgar Lilienfeld (Canada 1925, United States 1926 and 1928) and by Oskar Heil (1934), but no working device was built then, and Bell Labs' lawyers advised against naming Shockley inventor of a field-effect patent because the idea was not new.

name: Integrated circuit
note: Robert Noyce at Fairchild Semiconductor made the first practical monolithic chip about six months later.

name: ARPANET
note: Its packet switching drew on Donald Davies’ work at Britain’s National Physical Laboratory, whose network came first.

name: Shadoof
note: Some historians hold that it began on the Nile, citing tomb drawings at Thebes from 1250 BCE; another theory, with little evidence, places its origin in India.

name: Noria
note: Some accounts date the noria proper from around 300 CE, when the Romans replaced its wooden compartments with ceramic pots tied to the outside of an open-framed wheel.

name: Canning
people: Nicolas Appert; Peter Durand; Bryan Donkin
note: The Dutch navy was reported to carry salmon in tin-plated iron boxes as early as 1772; the tin can patented by Durand in 1810 was allegedly the idea of the Frenchman Philippe de Girard.

name: Mechanical reaper
people: Patrick Bell; Obed Hussey; Cyrus McCormick
note: Gallic reapers, which combed off the heads of grain, were used in Roman times in what is now France. Cyrus McCormick claimed to have invented his reaper in 1831, and an 1861 ruling of the United States Patent and Trademark Office gave much of the credit to Obed Hussey.

name: Tractor
people: John Charter; John Froelich; Dan Albone
note: Steam came first: Thomas Aveling made a portable engine self-propelled in 1859, and steam ploughing engines, used in pairs to haul a plough by cable, were the first tractors.

name: Barbed wire
people: Louis François Janin; Lucien B. Smith; Joseph Glidden
note: Lucien B. Smith, who received the first United States patent in 1867, is regarded as the inventor; Leonce Eugene Grassin-Baledans had proposed a pointed wire fence in France in 1860.

name: Aquaculture
independent_origins: Alekoko, Hawaii at least 1,000 years ago
note: The Gunditjmara of south-western Victoria, Australia, may have raised eels at Budj Bim as early as about 4,580 BCE, though Peter Sutton disputes that their eel traps were aquaculture. Evidence from Jiahu in China, from 6200 BCE, is speculative.

name: Wine
note: Pottery jars from Jiahu in China, of the early seventh millennium BCE, may have held a fermented drink of rice and grapes, but other fruits cannot be ruled out. The Hajj Firuz jars from Iran, of about 5000 BCE, are also called the earliest firm evidence of wine production.

name: Cheese
note: Holed pottery from pile-dwellings on Lake Neuchatel in Switzerland, roughly eight thousand years old, is thought to come from cheese strainers; where cheese-making began is not known.

name: Coffee
note: The 10th-century physician al-Razi wrote of bunchum, which later accounts say was made from a root. Legends credit the discovery to Kaldi, a 9th-century goatherd, or to the 13th-century Sufi al-Shadhili.

name: Seismoscope
note: Unverified claims that a device resembling an earthquake detector existed in Ancient Egypt have no confirmation in reliable historical sources. How the central column inside the vessel opened only one dragon's mouth is not known.

name: Water clock
independent_origins: Babylon 16th century BCE; Greater Iran 500 BCE; China 6th century BCE
note: The use of water clocks in Babylonian astronomy is traced back to the Old Babylonian Empire (c. 2000–1600 BCE), and N. Narahari Achar and Subhash Kak suggest their use in India as early as the 2nd millennium BCE from the Atharvaveda.

name: Armillary sphere
note: Joseph Needham traced the Chinese armillary sphere to the single-ring instrument of Shi Shen and Gan De in the 4th century BCE, a dating that Christopher Cullen rejects.

name: Barometer
note: The 1643 date was suggested only after Torricelli's death. Gasparo Berti built a rudimentary water barometer between 1640 and 1644, and René Descartes described an experiment to measure atmospheric pressure as early as 1631, with no evidence that he built one.

name: Thermometer
note: Galileo is often said to be the inventor, but no surviving document shows that he made such an instrument. Jean Leurechon described one with a scale of 8 degrees in 1624.

name: Kite
note: The kite has been claimed as the invention of the 5th-century BCE Chinese philosophers Mozi and Lu Ban, who are said to have flown wooden kites called muyuan.

name: Lathe
note: Tenuous evidence of a turned artifact at a Mycenaean Greek site may go back to the 13th or 14th century BCE.

name: Loom
note: The warp-weighted loom may have originated earlier, in the Neolithic period.

name: Sewing needle
note: Bone awls from Blombos Cave in southern Africa date to 73,000–70,000 years ago, and a point from Sibudu Cave in South Africa, 61,000 years old, might be from a bone needle.

name: Pencil
note: Some sources date the discovery of the Borrowdale graphite as early as 1500.

name: Wheelbarrow
note: The Records of the Three Kingdoms credit Zhuge Liang with its invention in 231 CE; M. J. T. Lewis read a 'one-wheeler' in temple inventories at Eleusis of 408–406 BCE as a Greek wheelbarrow, but there is no evidence for it in Greece or Rome.

name: Hot-air balloon
note: Sky lanterns, used for military signals by Zhuge Liang in the Three Kingdoms era, were a precursor; in 1709 Bartolomeu de Gusmão showed an unmanned demonstration of his Passarola to John V of Portugal at the Casa da Índia.

name: Parachute
people: Francesco di Giorgio Martini; leonardo-da-vinci; Louis-Sébastien Lenormand
note: In 852 Armen Firman jumped from a tower in Córdoba wearing a large cloak; Faust Vrančić's jump of 1617 from St Mark's Campanile in Venice probably never took place. The first recorded jump with a parachute was Lenormand's in 1783.

name: Helicopter
people: Jacques Breguet; Louis Breguet; Paul Cornu
note: Hermann Ganswindt's helicopter may have carried people in Berlin-Schöneberg in July 1901, but the film of the flight is lost; the Breguet machine was held steady by a man at each corner, so Cornu's flight of 13 November 1907 is reported as the first free one.

name: Junk
note: A pottery model of a ship with a stern-mounted rudder from before the 1st century CE is already called a junk; the battened junk sail was probably Southeast Asian in origin, first shown at the Bayon temple at Angkor Thom.

name: Dugout canoe
independent_origins: Dufuna, Nigeria c. 8,000 years ago; Kuahuqiao, Zhejiang, China c. 8,000 years ago
note: Dugouts may be the oldest boats found only because their massive wood survives better than lighter craft such as bark canoes.

name: Horseshoe
note: Four bronze horseshoes with what seem to be nail holes, found in an Etruscan tomb of around 400 BCE, may be older, and Catullus's 'mule shoes' may mean the Roman hipposandal rather than a nailed shoe; there is no hard evidence that the Druids invented it.

name: Spear-thrower
note: It may be older: it is believed to have been in use from around 30,000 years ago, and the arthritic right elbow of Mungo Man, of 42,000 BP, has been read as 'atlatl elbow'.

name: Bayonet
note: The word bayonette is older, from the 16th century, but it is unclear whether it then named a knife fitted to a gun; its supposed origin in the town of Bayonne has no basis in fact.

name: Torpedo
note: Around 1280 Hasan al-Rammah described a rocket-driven incendiary craft that moved across the water, often cited as an early torpedo, but historians class it as a surface-skimming rocket; until about 1900 the word also covered mines and spar torpedoes.

name: Rifling
note: Gaspard Kollner of Vienna made spiral-grooved barrels as early as 1498 by some accounts, but some scholars hold that his grooves were straight until Kotter helped him.

name: Crane
note: The shaduf of ancient Mesopotamia is sometimes counted as the first crane, but it was a lever for lifting irrigation water.

name: Typewriter
note: Historians estimate that some form of typewriter was invented 52 times: a British patent of 1714 granted to Henry Mill appears to describe a similar machine, and Pellegrino Turri built one for a blind friend between 1801 and 1808.

name: Phonograph
note: The phonautograph, patented in 1857 by Édouard-Léon Scott de Martinville, recorded sound but could not play it back, and Charles Cros described a way of reproducing sound in a sealed letter of April 30, 1877, which he later had read to claim priority of conception.

name: Morse code
note: The alphabet that carries Morse's name was Alfred Vail's, who extended Morse's numerals-only design in 1840, and most of the present international code comes from Friedrich Gerke's revision of 1848.

name: Radar
people: Christian Hülsmeyer; Robert M. Page; Robert Watson-Watt
note: Radar was developed in secret by several countries before and during World War II; Heinrich Hertz had shown in 1886 that radio waves reflect from solid objects, and the first pulsed systems were shown in the United States in 1934 and in Germany and Great Britain in 1935.

name: Personal computer
note: Which machine was the first personal computer is disputed: PC Magazine called IBM's SCAMP prototype of 1973 the world's first personal computer, the MCM/70 of 1973 is described as the first personal desktop microcomputer, and many consider the Altair 8800 of 1974 the first true one.

name: Transatlantic cable
place: Valentia Island, Ireland, to Trinity Bay, Newfoundland
credited_to: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland; United States
people: Cyrus West Field; Charles Tilston Bright; William Thomson

name: Library of Ashurbanipal
note: A similar library was found in 1849 in the palace of Sennacherib (705–681 BCE), and because the tablets of the two were mixed after reaching Europe, the contents of each can hardly be reconstructed.

name: Fired brick
note: Fired bricks are also said to have been used only since c. 4000 BCE. In China proper brick construction of walls and vaults emerged only in the third century BCE.

name: Flying buttress
note: The flying buttress was first developed in late antiquity: early, undated examples stand on the Basilica of San Vitale in Ravenna and the Rotunda of Galerius in Thessaloniki.

name: Reinforced concrete
people: François Coignet; William B. Wilkinson; Joseph Monier
note: Coignet seems to have used the iron to keep monolithic walls from overturning rather than to add strength; Wilkinson’s reinforcement of 1854 shows knowledge of tensile stresses.

name: Portland cement
note: The name Portland cement was recorded in a directory of 1823 with a William Lockwood. Aspdin’s cement has been called a proto-Portland cement: his son William is regarded as the inventor of the modern form, and Isaac Charles Johnson claimed to be its real father.

name: Hypocaust
note: The earliest reference suggests that the Temple of Ephesus was heated in this way in 350 BCE, and Garrett G. Fagan has disputed Orata’s priority.

name: Vulcanization
note: Thomas Hancock took out a British patent for vulcanization with sulfur on 21 November 1843, eight weeks before Goodyear’s US patent of 30 January 1844; accounts differ on whether Hancock had studied samples of Goodyear’s rubber.

name: Friction match
people: John Walker; Isaac Holden; Charles Sauria
note: Walker may have made his first friction matches during experiments in 1826. Earlier French friction lighters, Cagniard de la Tour’s phosphorus bottle of 1810 and François Derosne’s briquet phosphorique of 1816, proved inconvenient and unsafe.

name: Egyptian blue
note: The pigment is also said to have been first synthesised in the Fourth Dynasty. Whether its presence beyond Egypt reflects its spread or parallel invention is unclear.

name: Lacquerware
note: The Kakinoshima pieces are also dated to the 9th millennium BCE, and a lacquer tree of the Jōmon period is 12,600 years old. Experts are divided on whether Jōmon lacquer was invented independently or derived from Chinese techniques.

name: Sulfuric acid
note: Al-Razi may have made it without knowing in a recipe of his Book of Secrets. An Arabic treatise with a recipe for it, falsely attributed to Ja'far al-Sadiq, is dated to the thirteenth century by Julius Ruska but earlier by al-Hassan.

name: Electrolysis
note: In 1785 Martinus van Marum reduced tin, zinc and antimony from their salts with an electrostatic generator without knowing the process, and in 1789 Adriaan Paets van Troostwijk and Jan Rudolph Deiman split small amounts of water; Johann Ritter also demonstrated it in 1800.

name: Hall–Héroult process
note: Some authors claim that Hall was assisted by his sister Julia Brainerd Hall, but the extent of her part has been disputed.

name: Blood transfusion
note: Lower's transfusion was between two dogs; the first from an animal to a human was Jean-Baptiste Denys's in France in 1667, and the first successful one of human blood James Blundell's in London in 1818.

name: Prosthesis
note: The wood and leather toe from a burial near Thebes, dated 950 to 710 BCE, is described as the first confirmed use of a prosthetic device, as it shows wear; before its discovery in 2000 the oldest known was an artificial leg from Capua.

name: Sulfa drugs
people: Gerhard Domagk; Josef Klarer; Fritz Mietzsch
note: Domagk's team found the drug, but its active compound, sulfanilamide, had been synthesised in 1906 and used in dye-making; a French team at the Pasteur Institute showed that Prontosil works by releasing it in the body.

name: Cardiac pacemaker
note: Mark C Lidwill's portable apparatus of 1926 in Sydney already paced the heart from outside the body, and Albert Hyman called his hand-cranked instrument of 1932 an artificial pacemaker; the first implanted one dates from 1958.

name: Organ transplant
note: Skin grafts are older: Sushruta used grafted skin to rebuild noses in the 2nd century BCE. The first successful kidney transplant is given as Joseph Murray's in Boston in 1954, though a timeline of transplants lists one by Richard H. Lawler in Chicago in 1950.

name: Electric motor
note: Andrew Gordon and Benjamin Franklin described electrostatic motors in the 1740s and 1750s, but these were never put to practical use; Faraday's device of 1821 was the first electromagnetic one.

name: Diesel engine
note: Critics, among them Otto Köhler and Emil Capitaine, claimed that Diesel had invented nothing new; Capitaine lost a patent lawsuit against him. Diesel may have taken the idea of air-blast injection from George B. Brayton.

name: Alternating current
note: Pixii's alternator came first, but alternating current became practical for power only with the transformers of the 1880s; from late 1887 Thomas Edison campaigned against it as too dangerous in the war of the currents.

name: Lithium-ion battery
people: M. Stanley Whittingham; John Goodenough; Akira Yoshino

name: Wind turbine
note: Wind had powered machines since the windwheel of Hero of Alexandria and the vertical-axle windmills built in Sistan from the 7th century; Friedländer's machine of 1883 was the first to generate electricity.
